# Slate

Slate is a film studio any agent can run. Every stage of a film is a `slate` command, every check is a gate, and
everything a film knows lives in its own folder, so any agent in any session can pick up exactly where the last one
stopped. This skill is the front door: it routes the request, runs intake, keeps the goal whole and hands each stage to
its craft skill.

Two words used throughout:
- **The owner** is the person Slate works for. They approve spend, the two sittings, the look, and anything published.
- **The requester** is whoever asked for this film: often the owner, sometimes someone they work with, sometimes an
  autonomous agent working for them.

# The four modes

A film's mode is in film.json (`slate new --mode`). The CLI enforces each mode's rules whatever an agent intends:
refusals come back with exit code 1 (refused) or 4 (spend refused) and say why.

**A film made autonomous stays autonomous.** `slate new` and `slate variant` record each film's mode in Slate's own data
folder, outside the film, and every rule (spend, keys, After Effects, the queue, review routing) judges the film by that
record, whatever its film.json says now. Only a person at their own Terminal changes it, with
`slate film set mode <mode> --by NAME --reason "…"`. An agent's attempt is refused and recorded, and an edit of
film.json changes nothing (`slate status` shows the mismatch). A derived film starts in its parent's mode.

## Supervised (the default)

- **Two sittings block:** pre-production (the checklist, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist, the look test)
  and the final cut. Stop at each and hand over.
- **Packets don't block:** hero moments, generated takes and sound proofs arrive in review packets the owner answers
  when they like.
- **Spend past the film's budget asks first.** The budget is a hard stop; the owner can record a raise.
- **After Effects finishes the film**, as an editable project plus the masters, and only on the owner's go. Ask them
  to save and quit AE before masters render; never quit it for them.

## Express

- A short film runs straight through to a review cut.
- Every approval that would have blocked earlier (checklist, claims, script, voice, look) is batched into the final-cut
  sitting. Nothing is skipped; it's just asked once, at the end.
- Use it for short pieces where the requester wants to see something before deciding anything.

## Draft

- No generated plates, a library voice, fewer motion-blur samples (4 instead of 16).
- For animatics, quick variants and trying an idea.
- **Never delivered as final.** A draft that becomes the real thing leaves draft mode and goes through the gates again.

## Autonomous (agents working for the owner, such as Oneiro's pursuits)

- **Brands:** only brands whose four references are approved.
- **Claims:** only from the brand's approved-claims list. A new claim parks the film with a question for the owner.
- **REVIEW verdicts park the film** with their evidence, and never count as passes. Only a person releases it.
- **Spend** is capped monthly in Slate's own budget file, which the CLI enforces whatever film.json says, and backed by
  vendor caps

**Never for brand work.** A brand's film goes through Slate even when the ask says "a quick Higgsfield clip for
<brand>'s launch". Stylized generated clips aren't the brand's type, colour or real UI, and the fast lane skips truth,
claims, the ledger and take judging. Say that in one line, then run a short production: express mode suits it, with
`--generation where-it-helps` when the requester wants generated footage.

## UI recordings go to video-verifier

"Screen-record the sign-up flow in the Simulator and check the transitions frame by frame" is QA of an app, not a film.
Load video-verifier, not Slate. Its web recordings go through Aside, never another browser.

A **product demo film** that uses real app footage is Slate's: the footage comes from `slate capture ios` or
`slate capture web`, conformed to the film's clock and beat-mapped to the voice (slate-build).

## Editing and reviewing

- **Editing a Slate film:** notes on approved work are a revision of that exact artifact (perfect, don't replace); a
  cut-down, a new aspect or a new language is a derived film (slate-finish).
- **Editing an outside video:** `slate analyze <video>` breaks it down (transcript, scenes, measured eases); then either
  rebuild it as a Slate film or, for a trivial trim, make the trim and say that's all it was.
- **Reviewing a cut:** a Slate film's review packet comes from `slate review`; an outside film gets `slate analyze` and
  the review checklist in slate-qa.

## Posting and publishing

Nothing publishes itself. A request to post a film is refused unless the owner approved that exact file: its SHA-256
matches their approval, and the delivery manifest marks it approved for publishing. When either is missing, say exactly
which approval is missing and stop. Don't upload it anywhere, don't open a site to post it, and don't take any other
committing action on the requester's behalf.

## Out of scope in this version

Shooting live action, and audio description. Say so, then offer what Slate can make: a film from real app captures,
generated real-world shots where the generation setting allows, or captions and a transcript.

## When a vendor skill keeps winning

If Higgsfield's (or any vendor's) skill keeps taking requests Slate should get, adjust Slate's own trigger (the skill
descriptions), with the owner's one-time permission, and re-run the routing evals. Never delete or edit a vendor skill.

# slate-generate

Generated shots can lift a film or cheapen it. On the first films, generated pixels where code or real footage belonged
read as AI and were rejected; generated atmosphere, used carefully, earned its place. So Slate generates rarely by
default, only what code can't make, judges every take, and never ships an ugly one.

This is stage 8 of the production. Every generation runs on the Higgsfield **Cloud API** (the one funded lane), through
Slate's ledger, estimated first.

## 1. When to generate

- **The requester decides how much**: each film has a generation setting, `none`, `rarely` (the default) or
  `where-it-helps`.
- **Code first for anything designed**: UI, type, data, charts, logos and brand graphics are drawn by code, always. A
  generated plate never carries UI, text, charts or logos.
- **Generation is for what code can't make**: real-looking people, a real place or scene, a stock-style shot. On
  `where-it-helps` it can also be used where it genuinely adds something, or as a matte (its shape only), each with a
  written reason.
- **Drafts use no plates.** Autonomous films may generate under the same rules, but every generation waits for the
  owner's yes.
- **Generated people on screen need the requester's sign-off**, and a generated shot never implies a claim or a
  testimonial.

See [policy](references/policy.md).

## 2. Ask for it in the script

- `slate timing` writes `timing/shots.json`, `vo_cues.json`, `vo_words.json`, `events.json` and `timeline.json`. It

- Word timings come from Whisper by default; a word lookup never throws, it falls back to an estimate and records a
  miss. The miss list must be empty before any act is handed in (slate-build).
- Once an act render is registered the timing locks; only the owner can decide to re-time, with a reason.

## 7. Handing over to the pre-production sitting

When the script builds clean (and the treatment, the truth pack and the voice shortlist are ready), stop. The
pre-production sitting approves the checklist, the claims, the script, the voice shortlist and, when the brand's look
isn't approved, the look test. Say what's ready, where it is (SCRIPT.md, the truth pack, the casting reel), and what
each decision is. Record the owner's calls on the draft (trims, keeps, confirmations) as numbered decisions in the
tracker, with their words.

## Rules that hold everywhere

- One hand-edited source. Never edit storyboard.json, SCRIPT.md or the timing files; change script.json and rebuild.
- Nothing is invented: every UI element, word and number maps to a citation (truth packs).
- No invented testimonials or customer quotes presented as real; quotes carry who said them and a pinned source.
- Runtime stays within 10% of the target unless the requester asks otherwise or you justify it in the tracker.
- The picture can be restaged freely by builders; the words, beats and timing are the script's.

## References

- [truth](references/truth.md): researching truth; pinned sources; product-truth and capability-brief templates.
- [truth-packs](references/truth-packs.md): the rules every line and frame obeys about claims, data and the product.
- [treatment](references/treatment.md): the treatment template and how to write each part.
- [structure](references/structure.md): story shapes that work: bookends, payoffs, journeys, the end card.
- [script-as-data](references/script-as-data.md): script.json field by field, a worked example, the gates and fixes.
- [vo-writing](references/vo-writing.md): pace, read time, density, numbers, brand words, a character's own words.
- [signature-moments](references/signature-moments.md): the visionary bar and one signature moment per act.

Before building, compare the candidate routes for the film (built in code with the Remotion kit, built in After
Effects, the open web renderer, generation for real-world shots), recommend one, and timebox a test of the strongest
alternative if it's a close call. Record the choice and the owner's approval. The engine can be chosen per brand or per
act during look development.

## One clock

Every beat is keyed to the voice's words, and picture and sound read the same resolved timeline. So a full re-voice
re-times the film automatically; the renders and the mix still have to be rebuilt, and `slate make <target>` rebuilds
only what's stale, in order. `slate make all` goes through to delivery; `slate make --list` shows each node's state
without running anything.

## Keeping intention across parallel versions

Intentionality degrades when several films or acts are built at once. Tie every move to a word or an idea, prefer fewer
and better moves, and judge new work against the best earlier film's code and notes. Hold masters until the pass is
done.

## Machines

- Render locally, one heavy job at a time, through the queue. Never on a borrowed machine or the owner's work computer.
- Too much parallel rendering thrashes a Mac: six builders plus finals once drove the load to 293 on 14 cores. The
  queue's per-resource locks and its load guard exist for this.
- Keep heavy media out of cloud-synced folders; films live in `~/Movies/Slate/` by default for that reason.
- Never edit a shell script while a job is running it (zsh reads scripts incrementally).
- One copy of any MCP client at a time: two copies ran every action twice.

## Evaluating a suggested tool

When someone suggests a library, an MCP server or a skill, check it quickly and record the verdict with reasons: does
the repository exist, does it do what it claims, does it write files or only play live, would it open a browser, does
it need system permissions (those installs go to the owner)? See dependencies.md.

name: visionary
description: Think like a visionary — reframe the problem, generate radically non-obvious ideas across many lenses, kill the median, and push one to a distinctive signature (a feature, look, interaction, or experience no ordinary person or typical AI would land on). Use when Quinn says "visionary", "be a visionary", "think outside the box", "go above and beyond", "blow me away", "wow me", "what would make this legendary/iconic", "give me something nobody's seen"; or in any hard brainstorm / concept / naming / product-direction / signature-UX session where the obvious answer isn't good enough.
---

# Visionary

Quinn invokes this when the safe, correct, median answer is a failure. The goal is
work that makes someone stop — a feature, a look, an interaction, an experience
that "no ordinary person or typical AI would think of." Ordinary AI brainstorming
loses because it returns the *center of the distribution*: the ten things anyone
would list. Visionary means deliberately leaving that center.

**The bar (hold everything to it):** would this make Quinn say *"I've never seen
that"* — and want to build it tonight? Three tests every surviving idea must pass:
1. **Visceral** — a first-glance gut hit; you feel it before you analyze it.
2. **Non-obvious** — a typical person/AI would not have produced it; it required a
   reframe, an analogy, or an inversion to reach.
3. **Real** — specific enough to build or draw, with the insight that makes it
   special nameable in one sentence. A vague "AI-powered X" is not an idea.

Anchor taste to Quinn's north star — **The Browser Company (Arc/Dia)**: craft,
warmth, personality, physical/springy motion — the *feeling*, expressed inside the
project's own tokens, never by copying a brand. (See `~/.claude/memory/` design
notes and the relevant taste skill: `frontend-design`, `[company]-frontend-taste`,
`swiftui-taste`.)

## The method

### 0. Reframe before you ideate

The biggest visionary move is usually solving a *better problem*, not solving the
stated one more cleverly. Before generating:
- State the request as a job-to-be-done, then ask **"what's the real problem
  behind this?"** and **"what would make this problem not need solving at all?"**
- Challenge the premise. If the ask is a proposed solution ("add a settings
  page"), find the need underneath ("the user never has to configure this").
- Name the **10× version**, not the 10% one: what would this look like if it were
  the best in the world at wh
[… 1,430 characters left out of the recording …]
transition).

For a genuine hard brainstorm — and when workflow orchestration is available
(ultracode / the Workflow tool) — **fan these lenses out in parallel** (one agent
per lens, generating aggressively), then a **taste judge** pass that scores every
candidate on the three tests and keeps only the top few. Parallel divergent
generation + adversarial selection is how you beat median output; don't simulate a
panel in one voice when you can actually run one.

### 2. Kill the median

Explicitly discard every idea a normal list would contain. If an idea would appear
on the first page of a Google search for "ideas for X", cut it. What remains are
the candidates worth Quinn's time. Say what you're cutting and why, briefly — it
proves you left the center on purpose.

### 3. Converge with conviction — no porridge

Do **not** average three safe ideas into a mushy compromise. Pick the one (maybe
two) that hit hardest and commit. For each survivor:
- Name the **insight** in one sentence (the reframe/analogy/inversion that makes it
  work).
- Make it **concrete** — the feature spec, the layout, the interaction, the exact
  signature moment. Draw it, mock it, or spec it precisely.
- Note the **risk** honestly and how to de-risk it.

### 4. Push the winner to a signature

Take the chosen direction and design the one detail that sets it apart — the thing
people will remember and describe to a friend. This is where visionary earns its
name: not the concept alone, but the executed, distinctive moment. If it's UI,
render/mock it and judge it by eye against the taste north star (and grade it with
the local design model when relevant — see the `design-model-build` skill).

## Guardrails

- **Grounded, not unhinged.** Visionary ≠ impossible. Every idea must be buildable
  in this stack and honest about cost; wild framing, real substance.
- **Distinctive over derivative.** Channel the *feeling* of masters and brands;
  never clone their assets, names, or trade dress.
- **Serve the actual goal.** Novelty that doesn't make the product better is
  decoration. The reframe must still solve Quinn's real problem.
- **One signature per surface, not chaos.** A screen/product gets one nameable
  bold move executed precisely — not ten competing gimmicks.
- **Then hand back to rigor.** Once a direction is chosen, exit visionary mode and
  execute it completely (`goal-fidelity` — build every part, verify, don't drop
  the details). Vision without follow-through is the other way to fail.

How it was checked; sources; what it knows; how it synthesizes and explains; what it suggests next; its guardrails;
**what is not true about it**; where this film differs from the product; and what the film uses. Every line carries a
source. Describe a character only with capabilities the owner treats as true.

### Reference analysis claims

When a film remakes or answers an earlier film, list every claim in the original that conflicts with the brand's
current website or product, and decide each with the claim authority before writing.

- Recheck an original's statistics against a current public source; cut or correct any that don't match.
- A figure from an older source that can't be verified goes to the claim authority before it's used.

# Models

Slate doesn't work without the best models, so the best one for each role is the default: recorded in `registry.json`
with the date it was verified, pinned per film at first use, and overridable per film (film.json `models`), per user
(`slate.toml`) or per shot (the generate block's `model`).

## Roles

The role follows from what a shot's generate block gives it:

| Role | When | Typical inputs |
|---|---|---|
| a still | no image, video or duration | a prompt |
| animate a plate | an `image` (and optionally an `end_image`), or a `duration` | a start frame, an end frame |
| style-locked from references | `reference_images` | several stills that set the look |
| extend a plate | a `video` | an earlier selected plate |

`slate plates plan` shows each shot's role, model and estimate before anything is spent.

## Routing

- **Keep a routing table and a plate review sheet.** Models differ in brief fidelity: on the first films one family came
  out painterly and off-palette, another broke the brief with an extra element, and a third matched the keyframes.
- **Resolution and length caps differ**: some video models stop at 720p; use a higher-resolution model for hero plates.
- **Availability varies**: a model can be temporarily unavailable. Have a fallback per shot.
- **Native frame rates differ** (plates often arrive at 24 fps); the conform handles it (plates.md).
- **Re-check the catalogue** at the start of a project and before assuming a gap: the catalogue changes monthly, and
  model knowledge in any agent is older than the catalogue.

## What the Cloud API can't do

- **Voice and music**: no voice or music models. Voice and music come from ElevenLabs (slate-voice, slate-sound).
- **Product-true UI or exact brand type**: generated UIs aren't the product; UI and type stay in code.
- Some app-only models and workflows (a cloud video editor, narrated explainer workflows) exist only on the app-credit
  side, which isn't funded (spend.md).

## Pinning

`slate gen run` pins a shot's model at first use. A registry refresh never changes a pinned film; re-pinning is
explicit, tested and approved, so a re-generation in week three matches week one.
